issues.failure_explanation: The frozen ODE for the i-th coordinate depends on all other coordinates x_j, j != i. Its solution therefore cannot, in general, be written as a function sigma_i(t,x_i) of t and x_i alone. For example, in R^2 with F_1(x,y)=y and F_2=0, the frozen x-equation is u'=y, whose solution is x_1+ty and depends on the frozen y-coordinate.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace sigma_i(t,x_i) by a notation such as sigma_i(t; x) or sigma_{x_{-i}}(t,x_i), making explicit dependence on the frozen coordinates.
issues.overall_effect: The definition of the one-dimensional splitting operators e^{tK_i} is ill-posed as written, and the coordinate-wise construction used later must be re-expressed with frozen-state dependence.
issues.title: One-dimensional subflow written as depending only on x_i
issues.why_classification: A local notational/definitional correction preserves the intended splitting construction and all substantive claims.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: the first $p$ Taylor coefficients coincide with the first $p$ Taylor coefficients of $$T(t)x=e^{t\mathcal{K}}x=x+t\mathcal{K}x+\frac{t^{2}}{2!}\mathcal{K}^{2}x+\cdots+\frac{t^{p}}{p!}\mathcal{K}^{p}x +\cdots.$$

issues.failure_explanation: The displayed estimate uses powers of V(0) in the remainder, but V(0)=I. A Taylor remainder for V(h)-T(h) when the first p coefficients agree must involve the (p+1)-th and higher derivatives or Taylor coefficients of V and T, not V(0)^{p+1}. As written, the inequality is not a valid Taylor-remainder estimate.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the displayed formula by a standard Taylor-remainder estimate involving V^{(p+1)}(0) and K^{p+1} (or the corresponding coefficient differences).
issues.overall_effect: The heuristic derivation of the order-p convergence estimate is mathematically incorrect, although the later rigorous estimates are attributed to cited theorems.
issues.title: Invalid Taylor-remainder estimate in equation order p
issues.why_classification: The repair is a local correction of a formal estimate using standard Taylor-remainder notation; it does not change the claimed orders.

issues.failure_explanation: The theorem states a Chernoff-type product formula for V(t) assuming only exponential boundedness, differentiability on D(K), and local bi-equicontinuity. It omits the standard requirement that V(t) tends to I at t=0 (at least on a bi-dense set, or strongly/bi-continuously for all x). The paper's own preceding Chernoff statement explicitly assumes V(0)=I. Without such a continuity/initial-value hypothesis, the product formula conclusion is not guaranteed.

issues.failure_explanation: The tables show nonmonotone and sometimes worsening RMSE as n increases for several higher-order methods. For example, in the Lotka-Volterra table the 10th-order RMSE increases from 5.77e-12 at n=100 to 1.43e-11 at n=1000 and 1.32e-09 at n=10000; the 14th-order RMSE also worsens. In the Van der Pol table, the 8th-order RMSE worsens from 3.64e-13 at n=500 to 7.87e-12 at n=1000. In the Lorenz table, the 6th-order RMSE at n=100000 is larger than the 3rd-order RMSE. Thus the prose claim that increasing iterations improves accuracy and that higher-order methods systematically enhance accuracy is not supported by the reported data.

failure_location.quote: This trend confirms that increasing the number of iterations improves the accuracy of the approximation, and higher-order methods further enhance this accuracy, particularly when the number of iterations is limited.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Revise the prose to describe the actual nonmonotone behavior, add a stability/roundoff discussion, or recompute the experiments so that the claimed trend is supported.
issues.overall_effect: The numerical-validation narrative is materially misleading; the tables do not establish the advertised monotone relationship between n, method order, and RMSE.
issues.title: Numerical prose claims monotone improvement contradicted by RMSE tables
issues.why_classification: The formal theory is unaffected, but the paper's numerical claims require substantive reinterpretation or new computations; this is more than a local wording fix.
